items.item: A pointer-chasing benchmark must create a true data dependency between consecutive loads, or an out-of-order core overlaps the misses and the result measures bandwidth rather than latency

at.step: Timing one load means breaking the overlap

items.item: The chase must traverse a single permutation cycle covering every slot, since multiple short cycles revisit a small cache-resident set and under-report latency

at.step: One cycle, visited in random order

items.item: The latency-versus-working-set curve forms a staircase: flat plateaus are levels, and the knee between plateaus is that level's measured capacity (M)

at.step: Predict: the shape of the latency curve
Reading the staircase

items.item: A strided-access sweep finds the cache-line size (B): cost per access is flat below the line size (several accesses share a line) and rises to a plateau once the stride matches or exceeds it

at.step: Predict: cost per access as the stride grows

items.item: Hardware prefetchers can mask or shift the measured knee by fetching ahead of the access pattern, so a stride sweep's apparent line size must be checked against known prefetcher behavior or defeated with random order

at.step: A prefetcher can hide the knee

items.item: The TLB is a separate cache from the data caches; a TLB miss (page walk) can occur even when the referenced data is already resident in a data cache

at.step: A second miss, hiding underneath

items.item: TLB reach equals entry count times page size, so larger pages increase reach without adding entries, which is why huge pages help large, pointer-heavy working sets

at.step: A second miss, hiding underneath

items.item: Comparing a sequential walk against a random walk over the same footprint isolates the prefetcher's contribution: the gap between the two curves is exactly what the prefetcher is hiding

at.step: Sequential vs random tells the prefetcher apart

items.item: Measured latency and block-size results from one machine describe only that machine; the qualitative shape of the staircase, not the specific nanosecond or byte figures, is what transfers across hardware

at.step: Back to the vector: count and clock agree

items.item: An amortized cost proof bounds a count of operations (such as element copies); it does not bound wall-clock time, because a single operation's real cost depends on where in the memory hierarchy it lands

at.step: Predict: why would the clock still spike?

items.item: Benchmark results should be reported as a distribution with tail percentiles (p50, p99, p99.9), not a single mean, because associativity, cache sharing and OS scheduling perturb individual runs

items.item: A fixed CPU frequency (no turbo or frequency scaling) is required for a latency benchmark's nanosecond figures to be meaningful at all
